summary.en: Stephen Miller is confronting his first crisis as White House chief of staff while the United States is deploying drones to strike ELN guerrilla elements operating inside Venezuela, adding external military pressure. Venezuela has pledged to finish repairs on the Colombia pipeline by March and is experiencing near-daily blackouts that leave more than half of its population without power, while some thirty-somethings in finance and tech are beginning to return. JD Vance and his oil donor deny a secret meeting before a raid on Venezuela, and a legal strategy is being pursued to free Nicolás Maduro. Aldo Torres notes that each barrel of oil extracted leaves a Venezuelan household in the dark, and a Panamanian journalist’s home was set ablaze and a Venezuelan intelligence chief’s lawyer was found dead in a Madrid storage room. Two battle-related deaths were recorded in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Stephen Miller konfronterer sin første krise som sjef for Det hvite hus mens USA sender droner for å slå til ELN-guerrillaelementer som opererer i Venezuela, og dermed øker det eksterne militære presset. Venezuela har lovet å fullføre reparasjoner på Colombia-røret innen mars og opplever nesten daglige strømbrudd som etterlater mer enn halvparten av befolkningen uten strøm, mens noen tretti-årene i finans og teknologi begynner å vende tilbake. JD Vance og hans oljedonor benekter et hemmelig møte før et raid på Venezuela, og en juridisk strategi blir forfulgt for å frigjøre Nicolás Maduro. Aldo Torres påpeker at hver fat olje som utvinnes etterlater en venezuelansk husholdning i mørket, og en panamansk journalists hjem ble satt i brann og en venezuelansk etterretningssjefs advokat ble funnet død i et lagringsrom i Madrid. To dødsfall knyttet til kamper ble registrert i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro as well as Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
